q: You're moving house and carrying some long items in your car. What does the law say about your load?
options: It MUST be secure and not stick out dangerously
It only needs securing on high-speed roads
Passengers can hold it in place by hand
It can overhang 3 metres without markers
explain: You MUST secure your load and it MUST NOT stick out dangerously. Make sure any heavy or sharp objects are secured safely.

q: You've put some heavy tools loose on the back seat of your car. Why is this dangerous?
options: They could set off the car alarm
They could injure someone in a collision
They'll make your tyres wear faster
They'll stop the rear doors locking
explain: You should make sure any heavy or sharp objects are secured safely. If there's a collision, they might hit someone inside the vehicle and cause serious injury.

q: You're setting off on holiday with a fully loaded car. Your handbook gives different tyre pressures for a full load. What should you do?
options: Let some air out for a softer ride
Keep them at the normal setting
Inflate them to the full-load setting
Check them only when you arrive
explain: Tyres MUST be correctly inflated to the vehicle manufacturer's specification for the load being carried. Always refer to the vehicle's handbook or data.

q: Your car is heavily loaded at the back for a long journey. What may you need to adjust?
options: Your speedometer
Your fuel gauge
Your engine idle speed
Your headlights
explain: Carrying a load or pulling a trailer may require you to adjust your headlights. Lights MUST be properly adjusted to prevent dazzling other road users, and extra attention is needed if the vehicle is heavily loaded.

q: You're stopped by the police because your load is insecure and likely to cause danger. How many penalty points could this carry?
explain: You MUST NOT overload your vehicle and you MUST secure your load. Causing, or being likely to cause, danger because of your load or passengers carries 3 penalty points.

q: You're taking your dog with you in the car. How should you carry it?
options: Loose on the back seat
On a passenger's lap in the front
Loose in the front footwell
Restrained in a dog cage or harness
explain: You should make sure dogs or other animals are suitably restrained so they can't distract you or injure you, or themselves, if you stop quickly. A seat belt harness, pet carrier, dog cage or dog guard are ways of restraining animals in cars.

q: You're giving friends a lift and there are more people than seats with seat belts. What does the law say?
options: Two children can share one seat belt
Adults can share a belt on short trips
Only one person may use each belted seat
Extra passengers can sit in the boot
explain: You must wear a seat belt if one is fitted in the seat you're using, and you're only allowed one person in each seat fitted with a seat belt.

q: You're carrying three children under 3, but there's no room for a third child car seat in the back. How must the third child travel?
options: In the back using an adult seat belt
In the front in the correct child seat
On an adult's lap in the back
In the back without any restraint
explain: Children under 3 must be in a child car seat. If there's no room for a third child car seat in the back, the child must travel in the front seat with the correct child car seat.

q: You passed your car driving test in 2015. What's the heaviest trailer you can tow on your licence?
options: 750 kg MAM
3,500 kg MAM
8,250 kg MAM
12,000 kg MAM
explain: If you got your licence from 1 January 1997, you can tow a trailer that weighs up to 3,500 kg maximum authorised mass (MAM). This is known as a 'category BE' vehicle. You MUST NOT tow more than your licence permits.

q: Your grandfather passed his car driving test in 1985. What combined weight of vehicle and trailer can he usually drive?
options: Up to 3,500 kg MAM
Up to 7,500 kg MAM
Up to 8,250 kg MAM
Up to 12,000 kg MAM
explain: If you got your licence before 1 January 1997, you can usually drive a vehicle and trailer with a combined weight of up to 8,250 kg MAM.

q: You're checking whether your car can tow a caravan. What is the 'gross train weight'?
options: The weight of the empty trailer only
The downward weight on the tow ball
The weight of the car with no passengers
The fully loaded car plus fully loaded trailer
explain: The gross train weight is the weight of the fully loaded car plus the fully loaded trailer, and it must not be exceeded. If your VIN plate doesn't list a train weight, you shouldn't use your vehicle for towing.

q: You're loading your caravan for a holiday. Where should you put the heaviest items?
options: Over the caravan's axle(s)
At the very back of the caravan
In the high roof lockers
All on one side of the caravan
explain: You should distribute the weight in your caravan or trailer evenly, with heavy items over the axle(s). This should minimise the possibility of swerving or snaking and loss of control.

q: You're hitching a loaded trailer to your car. How should the load act on the tow ball?
options: It should lift upwards on the tow ball
It should press down, within the maker's limit
It should put no weight on the tow ball
It should be as heavy as you can make it
explain: You should ensure a downward load on the tow ball. The manufacturer's recommended weight and tow ball load should not be exceeded.

q: You're towing a caravan on a dual carriageway when it starts to snake from side to side. What should you do?
options: Brake hard to stop quickly
Accelerate to straighten it up
Ease off and slow down gently
Steer sharply against the swing
explain: If the trailer starts to swerve or snake, ease off the accelerator and reduce speed gently to regain control. Don't brake harshly.

q: You're about to tow a caravan that's wider than the back of your car. What MUST you do?
options: Drive with your hazard lights on
Keep below 30 mph at all times
Have a passenger watch behind for you
Fit suitable towing mirrors
explain: If your trailer or load is wider than your vehicle, or it blocks your view behind, towing mirrors MUST be used. You can be fined and get 3 penalty points for towing without proper towing mirrors.

q: You're buying a trailer to tow with your car. Above what loaded weight must it have a working brake system?
options: 500 kg
750 kg
explain: Your trailer must have a working brake system if it weighs over 750 kg when it's loaded. Any brakes fitted must be in good working order.

q: You're hitching a trailer to your car. Why must you also use a breakaway cable or secondary coupling?
options: In case the trailer becomes detached
To power the trailer's lights
To stop the trailer from snaking
To reduce the load on the tow ball
explain: Your trailer MUST be fitted with a secondary coupling device, such as a safety chain. You must use a breakaway cable or secondary coupling in case the trailer becomes detached from your car.

q: You're towing a trailer behind your car. Which number plate must the trailer display?
options: The trailer's own registration number
No plate is needed on a small trailer
The same number plate as your car
A plate showing your home postcode
explain: You must display the same number plate on your trailer as on your towing car.

q: You're towing a caravan on a single carriageway road where the national speed limit applies. What's your maximum speed?
options: 40 mph
50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
explain: Cars towing caravans or trailers have a speed limit of 50 mph on single carriageways, unless signs show a lower limit. Reduced speed limits apply when you're towing.

q: Your car's maximum authorised mass (MAM) is under 3,500 kg. What's the longest trailer you can tow with it?
options: 5 metres
10 metres
7 metres
12 metres
explain: If your vehicle's maximum authorised mass is 3,500 kg or less, you can't tow a trailer that's longer than 7 metres. This doesn't include the A-frame.

q: Your friend's car has broken down and they ask you to tow it home with a tow rope. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: Use the rope and keep under 40 mph
Use the rope with your hazard lights on
Use the longest rope you can find
Consider professional recovery instead
explain: Towing a vehicle on a tow rope is potentially dangerous. You should consider using a solid tow bar or professional recovery.

q: You're towing a caravan and want to overtake a slow-moving vehicle. What should you bear in mind?
options: You'll be able to accelerate faster
The extra length will affect overtaking
Your stopping distance will be shorter
Other drivers must let you pull in
explain: When towing, remember the extra length will affect overtaking and manoeuvring. The extra weight will also affect braking and acceleration, and your stopping distance may increase significantly.

q: You're having a tow bar fitted to your car, which was first used in 2015. What must the tow bar be?
options: Type-approved for your car
Painted the same colour as the car
Fitted by a DVLA garage
Removable when not in use
explain: If you get a tow bar for your car, it needs to be type-approved, meaning it meets EU regulations and is designed for your car. It will have a label with an approval number and details of the vehicles it's approved for.

q: You've parked your car and trailer at night on a road with a 30 mph speed limit. What does the law say about lights?
options: No lights are needed on a 30 mph road
Only the car needs its sidelights on
The trailer MUST NOT be left without lights
The hazard warning lights must be left on
explain: Cars may be parked without lights on some roads with a 30 mph limit, but other vehicles and trailers, and all vehicles with projecting loads, MUST NOT be left on a road at night without lights.

q: You're choosing a trailer to tow with your car. What's the maximum width allowed for a trailer?
options: 2.00 metres
2.10 metres
2.30 metres
2.55 metres
explain: The maximum trailer width for any towing vehicle is 2.55 metres.
